When Fine-Grained Credit Assignment Helps and Hurts:
Multimodal Agentic Reinforcement Learning through Video Editing

Lei Zhao ††thanks: Part of this work was completed while Lei Zhao was an intern at Philo Labs. Emails, in author order: leizhao7@upenn.edu, tom@philolabs.ai, and christine@philolabs.ai.    Zongheng Cao Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania  Philo Labs    Xinyu Hu Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania  Philo Labs
Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for training multimodal agents to reason and use tools. However, it remains unclear when fine-grained credit assignment improves learning and when it fails to improve task performance. Video editing provides a useful testbed for this question, combining multimodal perception, long-horizon planning, and tool use with delayed outcome feedback. We construct four movie-trailer editing task types—Content Selection, Narrative Sequencing, Rough Cut, and Fine Cut—that reflect real-world editing workflows and span different levels of task complexity and interaction horizon. Decaying process rewards provides the largest benefit on Fine Cut, with a 45.4% relative gain over outcome-only GRPO on tasks averaging more than 60 turns under outcome-only GRPO. On the three shorter-horizon task types averaging 30–40 turns under the same baseline, outcome-only GRPO remains competitive, with decaying process rewards yielding at most a 10.4% relative gain. Process rewards from an LLM judge initially improve tool use and encourage visual inspection. As training progresses, however, GRPO+PRM with a fixed process-reward weight increasingly exhibits excessive reasoning and redundant tool calls: process rewards continue to rise while task completion rates and outcome scores decline. Decaying the process-reward weight to zero mitigates this reward-hacking behavior while preserving the early gains. Despite dense token-level supervision, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) yields little improvement or substantial degradation and is highly sensitive to the choice of privileged information. Our analysis reveals differences in teacher–student disagreement and gradient magnitudes, and suggests possible dilution of informative signals over long trajectories.

when-fine-grained-credit-assignment-helps-and-hurts

1 Introduction

Video agents are moving from video understanding towards long-horizon multimodal tasks such as video production, where models must integrate multimodal perception, planning, and tool use (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Sandoval-Castañeda et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b). However, even the strongest agent systems struggle on these tasks (Cao et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026). Reinforcement learning has shown promise for improving their performance, enabling agents to refine their decision-making and tool-use policies through feedback from task execution (Kulkarni and Fazli, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2025d). However, reward formulation remains challenging because the quality of the resulting video rests on subjective judgment (Yan et al., 2026a; Wen et al., 2026). In addition, feedback on the final video becomes available only after a sequence of interdependent editing decisions, making it difficult to determine how individual actions contribute to the final outcome. Credit assignment is therefore central to training these agents (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2026). Yet it remains unclear when finer-grained credit assignment helps or hurts learning in long-horizon multimodal tasks.

Most work on video production builds a workflow around a model that it never updates (Sandoval-Castañeda et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b). Crayotter trains an editing agent with segment-level credit, where segments group consecutive editing events from the same stage (Yan et al., 2026a). We ask how trajectory-, turn-, and token-level credit compare across editing tasks under a shared training setup. Elsewhere, several lines report that finer credit helps. VAGEN gives a multi-turn visual agent dense turn-level supervision (Wang et al., 2025b), TAPO repairs the credit that a trajectory-level advantage misassigns to tool calls inside failed rollouts (Dong et al., 2026), and interface agents trained on step-level progress signals beat actors trained on outcome rewards alone (Zhang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025). Other work reports negative results for process rewards. Group-relative optimization with an outcome reward provably carries an implicit process reward, which makes an explicit one look redundant (Sullivan and Koller, 2025). A process reward is dense but remains prone to bias and reward hacking (Zheng et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). Outcome-only training is argued to suffice on long horizons once exploration is wide enough (Pu et al., 2026). How credit should be assigned in long-horizon multimodal agents therefore remains unclear.

We study the question in movie-trailer editing. We generate 797 tasks from 49 real movies and their released trailers. The work decomposes into four stages that a human editor performs in order, which give the task types Content Selection (CS), Narrative Sequencing (NS), Rough Cut (RC), and Fine Cut (FC). The four types differ in editing requirements, interaction length, and in the quality profile of the turns they elicit, which lets us ask how the same credit signal behaves as the task changes. We train Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) for 50 updates on 716 of these tasks under four schemes that cover the three granularities. At the trajectory level we use outcome-only GRPO. At the turn level we compare GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda) and GRPO+PRM (decayed λ\lambda). Both use a process reward from Gemini 3.8 Flash, averaged over three votes. At the token level we use on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). Its teacher receives privileged information that the student never sees: reference answers or turn-level suggestions. Outcome scores come from Gemini 3.1 Pro, so the process reward and the outcome reward never share a model. The schemes share the base model, training tasks, and number of updates, while objective-specific settings are detailed in Appendix C.1. We evaluate every run on 81 validation tasks four times and report the mean, and we record how the agent behaves as well as what it scores.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we develop a data-construction pipeline that turns films and their released trailers into four types of editing tasks reflecting real-world editing workflows. Training on these tasks improves Qwen3.5-9B’s video editing performance on held-out films. Second, we compare trajectory-, turn-, and token-level learning signals under a shared setup. Decaying process rewards yields a 45.4% relative gain over outcome-only GRPO on Fine Cut, while outcome-only GRPO remains competitive on the three shorter-horizon task types. Third, we analyze training dynamics and model behavior to identify limitations of the tested finer-grained signals: fixed process rewards can undermine task completion despite encouraging desirable behaviors, and OPSD is sensitive to the privileged information provided to its teacher.

2 Related Work

Agents for video production.

Video-editing agents have evolved from executing language-guided actions to managing long-horizon multi-stage production (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Sandoval-Castañeda et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c; Ding et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2026b; Liang et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026a). These systems focus on designing editing workflows while keeping the underlying models fixed. Despite this progress, advanced agents remain unreliable in professional video post-production tasks (Cao et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026). Another line of work trains video-editing policies (Tang et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026). These methods use policy gradients for shot composition or supervised and preference-based post-training for tool-using planners. Crayotter assigns segment-level credit based on rankings of finished videos produced for the same task (Yan et al., 2026a). Our study compares trajectory-, turn-, and token-level supervision across a shared suite of editing tasks.

Credit assignment for long-horizon agents.

Attributing delayed outcomes to the decisions that caused them is a long-standing challenge (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2021; Harutyunyan et al., 2019; Mesnard et al., 2020; Meulemans et al., 2023). Research on language agents builds explicit learning signals at several granularities. Trajectory-level methods score a whole rollout against its peers (Shao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025d). Turn-level methods estimate value, progress, or a relative advantage for each turn (Zhou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Feng et al., 2025; Xi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Tan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Finer methods assign an advantage to a reasoning step or a segment within a response (Kazemnejad et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Multimodal work follows the same three levels across visual, interface, embodied, and video agents (Wang et al., 2025b; Pang et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2025; Kulkarni and Fazli, 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c). Whether explicit finer-grained supervision improves learning remains an empirical question. Under mild assumptions, outcome-only GRPO can be written as a process-aware objective that carries an implicit Monte Carlo process reward (Sullivan and Koller, 2025). Process reward models are also hard to build and to evaluate. Synthesizing their labels by Monte Carlo estimation generalizes worse than using a judge or a human annotator (Zhang et al., 2025b), and benchmarks for fine-grained error detection expose substantial weaknesses in current models (Song et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026). Empirical studies nevertheless report benefits from denser feedback (Wang and Ammanabrolu, 2025; Wu et al., 2026), alongside failure modes involving teacher guidance, reward-model overoptimization, and proxy exploitation (Li et al., 2026d; Fu et al., 2026; Skalse et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023; Thaman, 2026; Pu et al., 2026; Gunjal et al., 2026; Shao et al., 2025). Evidence remains limited on when finer-grained supervision helps or hurts long-horizon multimodal agents, and how these effects vary across tasks and training stages.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Long-Horizon Multimodal Agent

We consider a task xx drawn from a task distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, in which an agent interacts with an environment over many turns, following standard formulations of long-horizon agentic RL (Zhou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025d; Feng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026c). At turn tt the agent observes a state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} and emits an action at∈𝒱∗a_{t}\in\mathcal{V}^{*}, and the environment returns the next state,

at∼πθ(⋅∣st,x),st+1∼𝒫(⋅∣st,at).a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t},x),\qquad s_{t+1}\sim\mathcal{P}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}). (3.1)

The state sts_{t} carries images, tool outputs, and a mutable workspace alongside the textual history. The episode yields a trajectory τ=(s0,a0,…,aT−1,sT)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},\ldots,a_{T-1},s_{T}) and a delivered artifact yτ=Output⁡(sT)y_{\tau}=\operatorname{Output}(s_{T}), which a grader maps to a terminal reward Rout​(yτ)∈[0,1]R_{\mathrm{out}}(y_{\tau})\in[0,1]. No reward is available before the agent commits.

3.2 Credit Assignment

We next present three credit assignment schemes at different granularities.

Trajectory level.

At this granularity we study Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) with an outcome-only reward. GRPO estimates advantages from a group of rollouts without a learned critic. For each task xx, we sample GG trajectories {τi}i=1G\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}} and score them with oi=Rout​(yτi)o_{i}=R_{\mathrm{out}}(y_{\tau_{i}}). The group-normalized advantage is

Aiout=oi−μoσo+ϵ,A_{i}^{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{o_{i}-\mu_{o}}{\sigma_{o}+\epsilon}, (3.2)

with μo\mu_{o} and σo\sigma_{o} the group mean and sample standard deviation. We optimize the policy using rollout importance sampling with token-mean reduction over valid assistant tokens (Appendix C). Every token of τi\tau_{i} receives the same AioutA_{i}^{\mathrm{out}}, so the signal does not vary within a trajectory. We write this setting as outcome-only GRPO.

Turn level.

A process reward model (PRM) scores each action from its interaction history and the tool feedback it produced (Wang et al., 2026). We average the MM valid judgments of a turn into ri,tr_{i,t} and add a normalized process term to the shared outcome term,

Ai,t=Aiout+λ​Ai,tproc,Ai,tproc=ri,t−μtσt+ϵ,A_{i,t}=A_{i}^{\mathrm{out}}+\lambda A_{i,t}^{\mathrm{proc}},\qquad A_{i,t}^{\mathrm{proc}}=\frac{r_{i,t}-\mu_{t}}{\sigma_{t}+\epsilon}, (3.3)

where μt\mu_{t} and σt\sigma_{t} are the mean and sample standard deviation of valid process scores at the same turn index tt across rollouts of task xx. We do not apply additional batch-level advantage normalization. We call λ\lambda the process-reward weight and compare two settings. GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda) keeps this weight fixed throughout training. GRPO+PRM (decayed λ\lambda) reduces it to zero partway through training. Later updates therefore use only the outcome reward. Every token of action ai,ta_{i,t} receives Ai,tA_{i,t}, so the signal varies across turns but not within one.

Token level.

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) matches a teacher distribution on the student’s own prefixes (Zhao et al., 2026b). The teacher πtea\pi_{\mathrm{tea}} is a frozen copy of the initial policy and receives privileged information ctc_{t} that the student never sees. We compare two forms of privileged information: reference answers and turn-level suggestions. For token kk of action ata_{t} we write pt,k​(v)=πθ​(v∣st,x,at,<k)p_{t,k}(v)=\pi_{\theta}(v\mid s_{t},x,a_{t,<k}) for the student and qt,k​(v)=πtea​(v∣st,x,ct,at,<k)q_{t,k}(v)=\pi_{\mathrm{tea}}(v\mid s_{t},x,c_{t},a_{t,<k}) for the teacher. All OPSD experiments use the forward KL divergence,

ℒ(θ)=𝔼t,k[DKL(qt,k∥pt,k)],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,k}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{t,k}\|p_{t,k})\right], (3.4)

taken over the generated assistant tokens. In practice we evaluate the KL on the teacher’s top-KK support rather than the full vocabulary, and Appendix C gives the details. OPSD trains on this loss with no reward term at all. Every token receives its own target, so the signal varies within a turn as well.

4 Task Suite

4.1 Tasks and Environment

We study movie-trailer editing as it is done in practice (Murch, 2001; Pearlman, 2012). We decompose the editing of one trailer into four stages that a human editor works through in order, following the workflow-oriented view of AgenticVBench (Cao et al., 2026). Each stage gives one task type, namely Content Selection (CS), Narrative Sequencing (NS), Rough Cut (RC), and Fine Cut (FC). Figure 1(a) illustrates the four editing operations. A task consists of a multi-turn episode in which the agent inspects the supplied media and commits its artifact. The released trailer provides a reference answer for each task, held by the evaluator and hidden from the agent. Table 1 gives the task, the input, and the output of each type of task. See Appendix A for the definition of each type and Appendix A.7 for two worked examples. Base scores range from 0.152 to 0.657 under the respective task metrics, and mean interaction horizons range from 15.3 to 87.2 turns.

Scoring.

Each task is scored on the artifact the agent commits when the episode ends. All tasks use the same three channels for this outcome score RoutR_{\mathrm{out}},

Rout=wdet​Rdet+wref​Rref+wblind​Rblind,R_{\mathrm{out}}=w_{\mathrm{det}}R_{\mathrm{det}}+w_{\mathrm{ref}}R_{\mathrm{ref}}+w_{\mathrm{blind}}R_{\mathrm{blind}}, (4.1)

where RdetR_{\mathrm{det}} is a deterministic verifier that scores the artifact against that reference answer, RrefR_{\mathrm{ref}} is a multimodal LLM judge that scores the artifact with that reference, and RblindR_{\mathrm{blind}} is the same judge asking whether the artifact works on its own terms. Both judge channels score against a weighted rubric, and one model call grades each rubric item with its own evidence attached. The weights of Equation 4.1 sum to one and vary with the type. In this paper, we use Gemini 3.1 Pro as the multimodal LLM judge. The process rewards used during training come from a different model.

Content Selection and Narrative Sequencing use only the deterministic score, with weights (1,0,0)(1,0,0). Content Selection scores the unordered selected shot set SS against the reference set S⋆S^{\star} using F1, 2​|S∩S⋆|/(|S|+|S⋆|)2|S\cap S^{\star}|/(|S|+|S^{\star}|). It evaluates selection alone, with partial credit for overlap.11 1 Selecting every candidate would yield a mean F1 of 0.478 on the 14 Content Selection validation tasks. Narrative Sequencing scores agreement with the reference order. Rough Cut uses (0.4,0.4,0.2)(0.4,0.4,0.2), combining deterministic cut-point similarity with reference-conditioned and reference-free judge scores. Fine Cut uses (0,0.4,0.6)(0,0.4,0.6) to assess sound design and transitions through the two judge channels. These task-specific metrics measure different editing objectives, so their absolute values are not a common scale of task difficulty. Table 16 lists the judge rubrics, and Appendix C gives the aggregation.

Editing environments and harness.

Each task runs in a fresh workspace holding the editorial brief, a manifest, and the media the task type exposes. The agent is provided with a shell and eight media tools for inspecting pictures, probing audio, and validating its own artifact. See Appendix B.2 for the full list. We run the agent in the official OpenCode harness. To keep training and rollout on the same pixels, we add a plugin to the harness that registers every image before it enters the conversation. See Appendix B for details.

4.2 Data Construction and Dataset

Given a source film and its released trailer, we detect shot boundaries and align usable trailer shots to their source-film footage. We partition the trailer into narratively coherent chunks and generate an editorial brief for each, describing its narrative role without identifying the clips. Each chunk yields one task of each type by varying the supplied media and required editing operation (Table 1). Figure 2 illustrates the pipeline, and Appendix A gives the construction details.

The pipeline produces 2,352 tasks from 49 films. After filtering with Gemini 3.8 Flash we sample 797 of them, 716 for training from 43 films and 81 for validation from 6 films that do not appear in training. Table 2 gives the split by task type, and Appendix A lists the films and describes the audit and the sampling protocol.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Training settings.

We train Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) for 50 updates on the 716 training tasks (Section 4.2) under four different schemes for credit assignment: (i) outcome-only GRPO, (ii) GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda), (iii) GRPO+PRM (decayed λ\lambda), and (iv) OPSD. For GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda), we use a process-reward weight of λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 throughout training. GRPO+PRM (decayed λ\lambda) keeps the same weight until update 20. We then decay it to zero over updates 20–30 and keep it at zero thereafter. Section 6.2 explains the choice of this interval, and Appendix C gives the decay schedule and full training configuration. For OPSD, we compare two forms of privileged information: reference answers and turn-level suggestions. Gemini 3.8 Flash generates the turn-level suggestions from the student’s context at each turn. These suggestions are provided to the frozen teacher as privileged information.

Evaluation.

We evaluate the final checkpoint of each run on the 81 validation tasks introduced in Section 4.2. To reduce evaluation variance, we evaluate every task four times and report the mean score, denoted avg@4. See Appendix C for the full evaluation configuration.

5.2 Experiment Results

Table 3 summarizes the results. Outcome-only GRPO improves all four task types, raising the overall score from 0.284 to 0.413. Unexpectedly, GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda) scores lower than outcome-only GRPO on every task type except Fine Cut. Decaying the process-reward weight improves all four task scores over GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda) and yields the highest overall score of 0.447. Its largest gain over outcome-only GRPO is on Fine Cut (0.293 vs. 0.201). OPSD (reference answers) performs similarly to the untrained model (0.277 vs. 0.284 overall), while OPSD (turn-level suggestions) drops to 0.044. Section 6 analyzes these contrasting outcomes.

6 Credit Assignment: Benefits and Failure Modes

We examine trajectory-level credit on long horizons in Section 6.1. Section 6.2 links process-reward hacking to declining task completion and studies process-reward weight decay as a mitigation. Section 6.3 examines the sensitivity of OPSD to privileged information.

6.1 Task Structure and Trajectory-Level Credit

Gains vary across editing tasks.

As shown in Table 3, outcome-only GRPO raises the overall score from 0.284 to 0.413. However, Fine Cut improves by only 0.050, whereas the other three task types each improve by at least 0.15. On Fine Cut, adding process rewards further raises the score from 0.201 to 0.239 with a fixed weight and 0.293 with a decaying weight. These improvements show that further gains on Fine Cut are achievable beyond the outcome-only result. On the other three task types, the tested finer-grained methods yield limited additional gains over outcome-only GRPO: none improves Content Selection or Rough Cut, and the largest gain on Narrative Sequencing is 0.052.

A possible explanation: long horizons mix good and bad turns.

To understand why outcome-only GRPO is less effective on Fine Cut, we evaluate every turn in the untrained model’s validation rollouts from the second evaluation repetition using Gemini 3.8 Flash. The judge labels each turn as positive, neutral, or negative. We quantify rollout mixing as 2​min⁡(n+,n−)/(n++n−)2\min(n_{+},n_{-})/(n_{+}+n_{-}), where n+n_{+} and n−n_{-} denote the numbers of positive and negative turns, respectively.

As shown in Table 4, Fine Cut has a mixing score of 0.651, whereas the other three task types range from 0.297 to 0.390. Trajectory-level credit assignment assigns the same advantage to every turn in a rollout and cannot distinguish between positive and negative turns. The higher mixing on Fine Cut is consistent with greater ambiguity in assigning credit to individual turns. This may partly explain the smaller gains from outcome-only GRPO on Fine Cut.

6.2 GRPO+PRM: Reward Hacking and Mitigation

Reward hacking with a fixed process-reward weight.

All task types except Fine Cut score lower than outcome-only GRPO, as shown in Table 3. Table 5 further shows a sharp decline in the model’s ability to deliver a result, with 44.1% of rollouts being truncated compared with only 0.3% under outcome-only GRPO. Late in training, the model continues calling tools to gather evidence but often stops before committing to a final result.

We further analyze the training dynamics of GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda). As shown in Figure 1(c), the process reward increases while the outcome reward declines after update 30. Appendix C.7 provides the full training curves. As shown in Section 7, process rewards encourage desirable behaviors such as visual inspection, reasoning, and reflection. One possible interpretation is that encouraging these behaviors helps improve task scores early in training. Later, continued optimization with a fixed process-reward weight may lead the model to overuse these behaviors, consuming its interaction budget and reducing its ability to complete the task.

Process-reward weight decay mitigates reward hacking.

Observations in Figure 1(c) motivate us to decay the process-reward weight λ\lambda to zero between updates 20 and 30. This schedule retains process guidance early in training and shifts later updates to the outcome reward alone. Results in Table 3 show that this approach is effective. On the first three task types, the model achieves performance comparable to outcome-only GRPO, with an average score of 0.568 versus 0.559. On Fine Cut, the method improves performance over the untrained model by 0.141, whereas outcome-only GRPO yields an improvement of only 0.050. As shown in Section 7, decaying the process-reward weight further encourages desirable behaviors, such as longer reasoning and more frequent reflection, compared with keeping the weight fixed.

6.3 OPSD Is Sensitive to Privileged information

With reference answers, OPSD scores 0.277, close to the untrained model’s 0.284. With turn-level suggestions, its score drops to 0.044 (Table 3).

OPSD gradients depend on privileged information.

The two variants share the same distillation loss, frozen teacher, student model, and training hyperparameters. Compared with reference answers, turn-level suggestions yield an approximately 15-fold larger mean forward KL divergence and increase the mean gradient norm from 0.0840.084 to 1.1771.177 (Table 13).

The OPSD signal can be diluted over a trajectory.

With reference answers, the most divergent 5%5\% of turns account for 47.4%47.4\% of the total KL but only 17.9%17.9\% of the tokens (Table 14). This concentration suggests that averaging over valid assistant tokens may dilute the contribution of the more divergent turns. However, KL measures disagreement rather than the usefulness of teacher guidance, and whether gradient magnitude or signal dilution causes the observed outcomes remains to be tested. Appendix C.5 provides further analysis of trajectory lengths, gradient norms, and KL concentration.

7 Model Behavior

Table 5 compares the behavior of the trained policies. We use outcome-only GRPO as the baseline for the GRPO+PRM variants and the untrained model for OPSD. Reflection counts turns with an explicit self-correction marker; it does not assess whether a correction is valid.

Process rewards encourage desirable behaviors but do not ensure completion.

Compared with outcome-only GRPO, GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda) encourages more visual inspection, longer reasoning, and more frequent self-correction markers (Table 5). However, these changes accompany higher scores only on Fine Cut; scores fall on the other three task types (Table 3). The truncation rate also rises from 0.3% to 44.1%. The value of these behaviors therefore depends on the task and on whether the model can still complete it.

GRPO gains accompany greater visual inspection.

Compared with the base model, outcome-only GRPO increases frames seen from 32.2 to 84.2, without increasing tool calls or reasoning length (Table 5). Greater visual input may help the three shorter-horizon tasks, consistent with their larger gains, whereas Fine Cut may require more complex tool use and reasoning to coordinate a longer sequence of editing operations.

Less process guidance mitigates hacking and elicits better behavioral patterns.

Compared with GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda), GRPO+PRM (decayed λ\lambda) makes fewer tool calls while retaining substantial visual inspection, producing longer reasoning, and showing more frequent self-correction markers (Table 5). These changes accompany a reduction in truncation from 44.1%44.1\% to 6.2%6.2\% and an increase in overall task score from 0.3340.334 to 0.4470.447 (Table 3). Compared with outcome-only GRPO, GRPO+PRM (decayed λ\lambda) achieves a substantial gain on Fine Cut, which may be associated with its longer reasoning and more extensive visual inspection.

OPSD behavior depends on privileged information.

As shown in Table 5, with reference answers, OPSD remains behaviorally close to the untrained model, apart from a lower blind rate. With turn-level suggestions, rollouts become much shorter, reasoning length and reflection frequency drop sharply, and blind rollouts become more frequent. These behavioral changes accompany the collapse in task performance (Table 3).

8 Conclusion

Our experiments show when finer-grained credit helps and when it hurts. Process guidance helps most on Fine Cut, while outcome-only GRPO remains competitive on shorter-horizon tasks. Process guidance can hurt when more visual inspection and reasoning accompany poorer task completion. Decaying the process-reward weight improves completion while retaining these behaviors. OPSD is sensitive to privileged information, showing that dense supervision alone does not guarantee effective learning. Our process-reward findings are based on GRPO+PRM with LLM-judged turn-level rewards on movie-trailer editing tasks; whether they extend to untested methods such as GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) and Turn-PPO (Li et al., 2026b) remains open. For OPSD, we identify failure patterns without establishing effective remedies. How to improve teacher guidance and training stability requires further study.
