Contents of the Appendix

Appendix A Task Construction Details

Figure 2 gives an overview of the data generation pipeline.

A.1 Corpus and Summary Statistics

Let

𝒟edit={(Fi,Ti)}i=1N,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{edit}}=\{(F_{i},T_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, (A.1)

where FiF_{i} is a source film and TiT_{i} is its corresponding trailer. The corpus contains N=49N=49 pairs, comprising 101.80 hours of source video and 2.09 hours of trailers. Instantiating four task types for every retained chunk produces an initial pool of 2,352 tasks, before task-level quality filtering and sampling. The final experimental dataset contains 797 tasks (Section 4.2).

A.2 Media Processing and Chunking

Task construction converts each long film and short trailer into localized editing problems. We normalize media geometry and create analysis proxies, then detect shot boundaries in both videos. A coarse-to-fine visual matching pipeline aligns trailer shots to candidate source-film moments and rejects low-confidence matches. Graphic cards, black frames, flashes, and other featureless intervals are separated from usable footage. Speech timestamps, music activity, and picture–sound relations are extracted only for constructing fine-cut tasks and hidden evaluation evidence; the finished trailer mix and its alignments are never exposed to the policy.

A semantic pass groups the trailer into broad story beats and then into local chunks that do not cross beat boundaries. The construction produces 622 raw chunks. We retain 588 chunks containing at least three usable picture clips and two source-film anchors. The source films contain 88,669 detected shots and the trailers contain 5,978 detected shots.

A.3 Construction by Task Type

The four tasks for a chunk are constructed independently. Narrative Sequencing uses the reference selection, Rough Cut uses the reference order, and Fine Cut starts from a reference rough cut rather than a sampled upstream output. This prevents one task type’s errors from dominating another task type’s training signal. The corpus therefore evaluates stagewise editing decisions; composing all task types into a fully end-to-end trailer editor is a separate setting.

Content Selection presents complete source shots rather than pre-trimmed positives and mixes them with neighboring and duration-matched distractors. In the final dataset, each task contains 21–36 candidates and 3–14 positives. Narrative Sequencing independently renames and shuffles the selected clips. Overlapping neighboring source windows are separated where possible so that the task cannot be solved by matching duplicate boundary frames. Rough Cut supplies the reference order but requires new in- and out-points for every clip. Matching ambiguity is retained as a timing tolerance, avoiding frame-exact penalties when equivalent boundaries exist.

Fine Cut begins from a stable rough cut and exposes production-sound handles, uncut dialogue candidates, an unaligned music window, and join metadata. The agent selects and trims dialogue, places music, chooses picture and sound transitions, and renders the result. Trailer-only picture is muted so that released dialogue and music choices cannot be recovered from its audio. The structured edit and rendered preview are evaluated together.

A.4 Task Inputs, Outputs, and Requirements

Each task package provides a local editing brief, the assets under initial_state/, and a public manifest.json describing those assets. The manifest identifies files and their local time coordinates; it is not an answer key. Hidden selections, reference orders, source–trailer alignments, and grading references are kept outside the policy-visible package. The four interfaces expose different decisions, as detailed below. Their scores use different criteria and should not be interpreted as a common difficulty scale.

Content Selection (CS): choose an unordered subset.

The input is a written description of the local trailer stretch and a pool of complete, silent source shots, with candidate IDs, file names, and durations in the manifest. Positive shots are mixed with distractors from the same film. Candidate numbering follows a shuffle and does not indicate relevance. The agent must screen the pool and decide both which clips to keep and how many to keep. It writes output/selection.json, containing a selected array of candidate IDs. Each selected ID is listed once; the order of IDs has no meaning. The task does not ask the agent to rank the candidates, order the selected shots, choose temporal boundaries, mix audio, or render a video.

The score is the set-selection F1 against the hidden selection: precision is the fraction of selected valid candidates that belong to the reference set, and recall is the fraction of reference candidates selected. An empty selection receives zero. The reference selection size is not supplied and is not a submission constraint; selecting too many clips is penalized through precision and selecting too few through recall. This is a continuous F1 score, not a binary task-success rate. The task grader additionally reports missed and incorrect clips; its diagnostic pass flag is separate from the reported score.

Narrative Sequencing (NS): order the supplied shots.

The input contains the reference-selected shots, independently shuffled and renamed, together with a description of the desired narrative stretch. Unlike the silent CS pool, the NS clips include production sound. The agent can use action continuity, dialogue, eyelines, movement, shot size, scene changes, and the brief to recover an ordering. It writes output/order.json, whose order array lists every supplied ID exactly once, from first to last. Dropping a shot, duplicating an ID, or introducing a new ID is invalid. The agent does not choose a subset, trim shots, or alter the sound mix.

The deterministic score combines three complementary properties of the permutation: one minus normalized positional displacement, the normalized longest increasing subsequence, and the fraction of directed reference-adjacent pairs retained. These three factors are multiplied. Thus, preserving some pairwise order alone does not ensure that the sequence preserves the reference joins. The Heretic chunk 5 grader used in our experiments accepts four explicitly enumerated orders and takes the best match among them; this is a task-specific repair rather than a general acceptance of arbitrary alternative orders.

Rough Cut (RC): choose an interval within every ordered clip.

The input supplies the selected clips in their reference order, their available durations, a local editing brief, and a target total duration. The agent writes output/cuts.json. Each object in its cuts array contains clip, in_s, and out_s. Times are measured from the beginning of the named source clip, rather than on a global film or output timeline. All supplied clips must appear exactly once and in the supplied order. Every kept interval must have a nonnegative start, an end after its start, and boundaries within the available media. The sum of the kept durations must stay near the supplied target. The agent chooses where an action begins and ends and how much time each shot receives; it does not reselect or reorder the material, add dialogue, or redesign the mix. The grading pipeline renders the submitted cuts for evaluation.

The final RC score combines a deterministic timing component (weight 0.4), reference-informed judgment (0.4), and judgment without the reference (0.2). The deterministic component is the fraction of scorable shots for which both the in-point error and the kept-duration error are within their reference tolerances. In-point tolerances are specific to each shot, reflecting matching ambiguity; they are not a universal frame-exact threshold. Shots with no source-film counterpart remain part of the required sequence but are excluded from this timing-component denominator. Submission validity and the full judging rubrics are detailed in Appendix C.

Fine Cut (FC): finish sound and transitions on a fixed picture edit.

The input is a reference rough cut with fixed shot order and picture timing. The manifest supplies shot durations, the times and identities of joins, available production-sound handles, an index of uncut dialogue takes, and an unaligned music window. These are candidate materials, not an assembled reference mix. Dialogue takes can contain surrounding speech, and some takes do not belong in the requested stretch. A shot made for the trailer can arrive without production sound; the prompt and manifest identify such cases.

The agent must deliver both output/edit.json and output/preview.mp4. The structured edit records the following choices:

  • •

    Dialogue: which supplied takes to use, the source-local in_s/out_s interval in each take, the output-timeline placement at_s, and any gain adjustment. Unneeded takes may be omitted; a take may be reused when the edit calls for it.

  • •

    Production sound: whether to retain or mute a shot’s own sound and, when a handle is used, its source interval and timeline placement. Silent shots cannot supply production sound that does not exist.

  • •

    Music: the offset within the supplied cue that aligns with the start of the edit, and the resulting audible entry and balance. The agent must determine the alignment from the material.

  • •

    Every join: a picture choice of cut, dip_to_black, dissolve, or other, and a sound choice of hard, carries_over, prelap, or under. These respectively distinguish a sound break, an L-cut, a J-cut, and a sound bridge. Every supplied join must be specified once; there is no quota requiring bridges or decorative transitions.

  • •

    Cards, when required by the task: text and appearance for supplied card placeholders. These are task-dependent, not a requirement to add a card to every stretch.

The picture shots and their established timing remain fixed, subject to the requested join treatments. The rendered preview must make the declared choices audible and visible and stay within the duration allowance used by the submission validator. Merely declaring a line in JSON does not establish that it can be heard in the final mix. The FC score combines judgment without the reference (weight 0.6) and reference-informed judgment (0.4); there is no deterministic exact-match component. The reference is one realized solution, and the rubrics evaluate task-appropriate alternatives through their actual audiovisual result.

A.5 Audit, Repair and Sampling

We audit every constructed task with Gemini 3.8 Flash, giving it the task description, the available tools, the video and audio assets, and the hidden grading references. The audit checks whether the brief is supported by the supplied media and whether the grading rules evaluate decisions that can be inferred from the public input. For Content Selection and Narrative Sequencing it checks whether visual and narrative cues support the target selection or order. For Rough Cut and Fine Cut it checks the feasibility of the timing, dialogue and audiovisual requirements, and it allows several reasonable edits.

Tasks with contradictory briefs, missing or corrupted assets, answer leakage, or unsupported reference constraints are repaired or dropped. A repair makes targeted changes to prompts, references, graders or media, followed by file-integrity, decoding and grader checks as applicable. Unresolved tasks and incomplete audit responses leave the candidate pool. Review coverage varies, and some candidates receive additional independent-context reviews while others receive a single audit or repair-author judgment.

Filtering and repair leave 925 candidates. We draw 797 of them by fixed-seed sampling stratified by split, task type and film, which preserves film coverage within each type and uses no policy reward scores. The 128 unselected candidates remain valid and are set aside only to fix the dataset size and the type proportions.

A.6 Split and Anti-Leakage Controls

The initial construction uses a film-level split: 43 films and 2,076 tasks in the training pool, and 6 films and 276 tasks in the validation pool. Filtering and sampling retain this film partition, yielding 716 training and 81 validation tasks. The 43 training films are 28 Years Later - The Bone Temple, A Complete Unknown, Arthur the King, Avatar - The Way of Water, Ballerina, Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, Bugonia, Challengers, Crime 101, Dune - Part Two, Evil Dead Burn, Furious 7, His Three Daughters, Hit Man, Horizon - An American Saga - Chapter 1, How to Train Your Dragon, John Wick - Chapter 4, Land of Bad, Lee, M3GAN 2.0, Maria, May December, Mercy, Migration, Mission Impossible - The Final Reckoning, Mufasa - The Lion King, Oppenheimer, Ordinary Angels, Ricky Stanicky, Send Help, Smile 2, Song Sung Blue, The Bikeriders, The Hunger Games - The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, The Iron Claw, The Marvels, The Rip, The Wild Robot, Transformers One, Warfare, White Bird, Young Woman and the Sea, Zootopia 2. The 6 validation films are Deadpool & Wolverine, Heretic, Sinners, The Drama, They Will Kill You and Whiplash. Candidate identifiers are independently randomized across task types, competing clips share a normalized encoding path, and answer records and reference alignments remain outside the policy-visible task package.

Table 6 lists the final validation coverage. Filtering does not require every held-out film to contribute a task of every type; for example, no Content Selection task from Deadpool & Wolverine is retained in this split.

A.7 Example Tasks

We expand the two worked task examples, Content Selection and Fine Cut, below and then provide additional Narrative Sequencing and Rough Cut examples. All four are actual validation tasks from the dataset used in our experiments. The task-specific prompts are reproduced in full, with only typesetting and JSON whitespace changed; the shared environment and tool instructions are omitted. File names in the prompts are relative to the task directory or its input asset directory. The JSON blocks are the format illustrations supplied in those prompts, not reference answers or completed submissions. In particular, the Rough Cut block lists only two placeholder intervals and the Fine Cut block lists only four of seven joins. An actual submission must satisfy the complete task requirements. The manifest details preceding each prompt report the actual supplied assets.

Content Selection: Heretic, chunk 1.

Dataset ID: s_1_heretic_c1; task-local ID: heretic_s1_c1. The public manifest contains 30 candidates (c01–c32, excluding c13 and c15), each with a path under initial_state/clips/ and its duration. The hidden reference contains 11 selected shots; this number is not supplied to the agent. The task asks for selection only.

Task — pick the clips for this stretch.

You are the assistant editor on the Heretic trailer. There are 30 candidate clips under initial_state/clips/.

This stretch of the trailer covers:

Two young women walk up a wooded driveway where their bicycles are parked and are greeted at the front door as the homeowner opens it. In the living room, a vinyl record spins on a turntable and the homeowner presents a closed copy of the Book of Mormon on the table. The conversation is warm with shared smiles and laughter across the room, concluding with him leaning forward at his desk speaking enthusiastically, followed by a close-up of the young woman on the couch reacting with an amused, questioning head tilt.

It sits inside the beat The Doorstep.

What to do.

Screen every candidate and pick the ones this stretch actually uses — the shots that cut together into the description above. The rest are real footage from the same film that the trailer did not use here; most are neighbouring shots from the same scenes.

  • •

    Order does not matter here. This stage is only about which clips.

  • •

    The count is not given. Decide it yourself; over-picking costs as much as under-picking.

  • •

    Every candidate is a complete shot at its own boundaries — silent, identically transcoded, numbered after a shuffle. Judge from the picture.

Deliverable.

Write output/selection.json:

{"selected": ["c03", "c07", "c19"]}

Just the ids you picked, in any order.

Fine Cut: Deadpool & Wolverine, chunk 3.

Dataset ID: s_4e_deadpoolwolverine_c3; task-local ID: deadpoolwolverine_s4e_c3. The manifest fixes a 12.867-second rough cut at 23.976024 frames per second, with shots p01–p08 and seven joins. Their successive durations are 1.272, 3.212, 1.835, 0.876, 1.001, 1.376, 1.377, and 1.918 seconds. The join times are 1.272, 4.484, 6.319, 7.195, 8.196, 9.572, and 10.949 seconds on the rough-cut timeline. Shot p06 is trailer-only and has no production sound; the other seven shots have sound handles extending four seconds on each side. Five dialogue candidates (d01–d05) and the music window complete the input.

Fine cut — deadpoolwolverine / c3.

You have a rough cut: 8 shots in order, each already trimmed to the frame, joined with 7 straight cuts. The pictures and their timing are settled and are not yours to change.

What is not settled is everything you can hear, and what happens at the joins.

This stretch covers:

Wide of the wasteland and Wolverine’s yellow-suit reveal in blinding light, cut into the birthday party for "I’m about to lose everything I’ve ever cared about," then back to the wasteland for the two of them going at it — "not my problem" / "is that what you said when your world went to shit?"

What you have.

  • •

    shots/pNN.mp4: the rough cut’s shots. They carry the film’s own production sound — whatever the microphone picked up on set.

  • •

    handles/pNN.m4a: the same sound, but running 4 seconds before each shot’s first frame and 4 seconds past its last. manifest.json gives handle.picture_in_s — where the picture starts inside that file.

  • •

    takes/dNN.m4a: 5 pieces of dialogue, lifted from the film uncut. manifest.json lists every stretch of speech in each file (speech_spans_s) — the line that was looked for, and whatever else happens to sit either side of it. All of it is yours to use. Not all of these pieces belong in this stretch.

  • •

    music.wav: the trailer’s music. The window runs wider than this stretch at both ends — how much wider is not stated — and it is not lined up. Where the music comes in is one of your decisions.

  • •

    manifest.json: shots, joins with their exact times and frames, dialogue index, music window.

The work.

Sound. The rough cut plays each shot’s own production sound, cut off hard at both edges. That is not a trailer. Decide what is heard:

  • •

    Which of the 5 lines belong in this stretch, and which do not. Some are here to be left out.

  • •

    Where each line you keep starts — under which shot, and how much of it runs before or after the picture changes.

  • •

    How much of a take to use. They run long on purpose; the trailer’s version of a line is usually shorter than the film’s.

  • •

    Where the production sound is worth keeping, and where it should give way.

  • •

    Where the music enters, and how it sits against the pictures.

Silent shots. p06 was made for the trailer rather than shot for the film, so it has no production sound at all — the picture arrives silent. What plays under it is entirely your call.

Picture. Most joins want a straight cut and nothing else — this is the common case, and adding something everywhere is the most reliable way to make a trailer worse. Where a join wants more, the moves are: a dip to black (how long it holds, and whether either side ramps, is part of the call), a dissolve, or something faster — a whip pan, a flash frame.

None of this is a checklist. Which of these a join wants — or whether it wants any — is the question being asked.

Deliverable.

Write output/edit.json:

{
  "music": {"starts_at_s": 3.20,
    "note": "file time that lands on 0.0 of the cut"},
  "dialogue": [
    {"take": "d03", "in_s": 1.40, "out_s": 3.10,
     "at_s": 0.00, "gain_db": 14,
     "why":
"carries into the second shot before the picture turns"
    }
  ],
  "joins": [
    {"join": 1, "picture": "cut", "sound": "hard"},
    {"join": 2, "picture": "dip_to_black",
      "black_hold_s": 0.30,
      "fade_in_s": 0.35, "sound": "under"},
    {"join": 3, "picture": "cut",
      "sound": "carries_over",
      "note": "line d03 runs on"},
    {"join": 4, "picture": "cut", "sound": "under",
      "note": "music holds it"}
  ],
  "production_sound": [
    {"shot": "p04", "keep": true, "gain_db": -6}],
  "cards": [{"shot": "p04",
    "text": "FROM THE DIRECTOR OF",
    "look": "white type, centred, on black",
    "in": "cut", "out": "dip"}]
}

take / in_s / out_s are which line and which part of it; at_s is where it lands on this stretch’s timeline, where 0.0 is the first frame. gain_db is how far you lift or drop it.

On levels. The music was mixed against a different set of lines than the ones you have, so it does not step aside where you need it to. Measured across the corpus, a take sits about 12 dB under the music bed, and dialogue that reads clearly usually sits 6–12 dB over it. Whatever you lay in will be buried unless you say otherwise — gain_db on the line, gain_db on the production sound, or both.

On each join:

  • •

    picture — one of cut / dip_to_black / dissolve / other

  • •

    sound — one of these four, and give it on every join:

    • –

      hard — the sound breaks where the picture breaks

    • –

      carries_over — something belonging to the leaving shot runs past it. An L-cut.

    • –

      prelap — something belonging to the arriving shot starts early. A J-cut.

    • –

      under — neither side’s own sound matters here; what carries the join is laid on top. A sound bridge — usually the music bed, sometimes a line from elsewhere running across both shots.

There are 7 joins, numbered 1 to 7 in order. Give all of them.

Also render it. Build the result as output/preview.mp4 — this stretch’s picture with your mix under it. It runs the length of the rough cut plus whatever black you chose to add. ffmpeg is here. The JSON says what you decided; the render is where anyone can hear whether it worked. A line you placed but cannot hear in the render is a line you did not place.

How this is judged.

Not against a single correct answer. The trailer that was actually cut from this material is one solution; a different set of choices can be as good or better. What is looked at is whether the choices hold together: does a line land where the picture supports it, does the music arrive somewhere that means something, is the restraint at the plain joins deliberate rather than absent.

Narrative Sequencing: Heretic, chunk 5.

Dataset ID: s_2_heretic_c5; task-local ID: heretic_s2_c5. The manifest supplies seven shuffled clips with production sound, k01–k07. Their durations, in ID order, are 9.215, 9.215, 8.881, 7.963, 5.752, 7.087, and 5.961 seconds. The output must be a permutation of these seven IDs; the IDs are not narrative positions.

Task — put this stretch in order.

You are the assistant editor on the Heretic trailer. The 7 shots this stretch uses have already been chosen and sit in initial_state/clips/ — but they are shuffled.

This stretch covers:

After the second press card, Mr. Reed is at his workbench assembling the architectural model of the house, followed by a close-up of his hands trimming a figurine with a craft blade. Next, Mr. Reed stands lurking in the shadowy hallway. Cut back to the two women confronting the test at the doors: Barnes crying in despair against the doorframe, and Paxton approaching the door marked "DISBELIEF". Finally, reaction shots of escalating dread: a tear falling down Paxton’s cheek, tightening to an extreme close-up of her throat swallowing as Mr. Reed describes the physical grip of fear.

It sits inside the beat Being Studied.

What to do.

Put the 7 shots into the order the trailer used.

Use all of them, each exactly once. The ids were assigned after a shuffle and carry no ordering information.

Judge from picture and sound: how actions run on from one shot to the next, dialogue continuity, where eyelines and movement point, how shot sizes step, where the location changes, and the narrative progression in the description above.

Deliverable.

Write output/order.json:

{"order": ["k03", "k01", "k05", "k07",
           "k06", "k02", "k04"]}

Every id, first to last.

Rough Cut: Heretic, chunk 2.

Dataset ID: s_3_heretic_c2; task-local ID: heretic_s3_c2. The manifest supplies 11 ordered source clips, p01–p11, with durations 3.698, 2.496, 3.674, 9.257, 9.840, 9.855, 2.339, 12.431, 18.185, 20.976, and 19.976 seconds. The exact manifest target is 15.182 seconds, rounded to 15.18 seconds in the prompt. Every clip needs its own interval. The numeric intervals in the prompt’s JSON block illustrate field syntax only and must be replaced by intervals within these actual source durations.

Task — rough-cut this stretch.

You are the assistant editor on the Heretic trailer. The shots for this stretch are chosen and ordered already, in initial_state/clips/ — 11 of them, p01 first.

Your job is to set an in point and an out point on each — where to start using that shot and where to leave it. Most run longer than the trailer’s use of them.

This stretch covers:

A run of dark close-ups — locks, a dial, ceiling lights from below — establishes the house as a maze. The two are led into the peaked-roof room with two doors side by side, and he tells them leaving means going out the back of his house.

Target total: 15.18 seconds across the 11 shots.

What to do.

For each shot, decide which part of it the trailer would use:

  • •

    where the action reads strongest — where to come in, where to leave

  • •

    whether to cut away mid-gesture or let it finish

  • •

    the lengths should add up to close to the target

Deliverable.

Write output/cuts.json:

{"cuts": [
  {"clip": "p01", "in_s": 12.34, "out_s": 13.90},
  {"clip": "p02", "in_s": 4.05,  "out_s": 5.20}
]}

in_s / out_s are seconds within that clip (the clip starts at 0). Give all 11, in order.

Appendix B Editing Environment Details

B.1 Episode State and Tools

Each task runs in a fresh filesystem workspace. The loader stages the task prompt, a manifest, and only the media visible for the current task type. The public manifest identifies the supplied assets and the timing information appropriate to that task. Prepared frames and observation tools support Content Selection, Narrative Sequencing, and Rough Cut. Fine Cut additionally requires manipulation of the supplied picture, dialogue, production-sound and music assets to build an audiovisual timeline and render a preview. Hidden answers, matching records, rubrics, and reference decisions remain in a separate evaluator-owned directory.

The policy may maintain notes, compare candidates, write timeline scripts, render intermediate results, inspect them, and revise its output. A turn is one policy generation request; it may contain several tool calls, so turn count and tool-call count differ. The episode terminates when the policy produces a final response or exhausts a turn, context, or output budget. The common turn limit is 100. Termination by a final response does not establish that a valid deliverable exists or that the task has been completed successfully.

B.2 Tools

Beyond the harness’s own shell, which provides FFmpeg, ffprobe and Python for local cutting, joining, mixing and probing, the policy calls eight media tools over MCP.

The policy interface supports text and images. The audio tools return analysis text rather than an audio waveform for the model to listen to. A transcript may drop words, so the absence of a transcript does not mean the absence of speech. The music tags come from a read-only store built before training, not from an online model. Audio onsets and periodicity estimates are candidates for editing decisions, not guaranteed musical beats. The technical validator does not provide the hidden outcome score or certify artistic quality. Thus observation and validation tools can reduce uncertainty while still leaving the editing decision to the policy.

B.3 Harness

Episodes run in the official OpenCode harness at version 1.15.5, commit d7a6e1da. We do not modify its binary or its upstream source. The media tools above are served over MCP, and an image-registration plugin on the tool.execute.after hook intercepts both native image attachments and MCP image content, normalizing and registering each image before it reaches the conversation history. The recorded configuration also disables automatic compaction and pruning and retains the policy’s original generation inputs for replay.

The plugin exists because the harness rearranges tool images into fresh user messages and may compress or trim history. Registering images ahead of that step keeps the request the inference backend receives identical to the one a training replay reconstructs, so the policy is never optimized against pixels it did not see. Images that arrive by URL, in an unknown binary modality, or without registration are refused rather than silently downscaled or dropped.

B.4 Deliverable Validation

At termination, the environment collects only the named deliverables: selection.json for Content Selection, order.json for Narrative Sequencing, cuts.json for Rough Cut, and edit.json together with preview.mp4 for Fine Cut. The submitted text response is not a substitute for these artifacts. JSON validation checks types, identifiers, finite time values and the schema required by the task. Missing or malformed deliverables and violated submission constraints receive zero outcome reward. Infrastructure failures and unavailable grades are tracked separately rather than automatically counted as policy failures.

Rough Cut checks.

Every supplied clip must occur exactly once and in the supplied order. Each retained interval must have a nonnegative in-point, an out-point after the in-point, and endpoints within the corresponding media. If the manifest specifies a target duration TT, the sum of all retained intervals must be within max⁡(1,min⁡(3,0.1​T))\max(1,\min(3,0.1T)) seconds of TT. This common delivery rule supersedes older total-duration tolerance text in the raw task prompt; it does not permit endpoints outside the source media. The original task-specific reference tolerances still define the separate deterministic quality metric (Appendix C.6).

Fine Cut checks.

The edit description must cover every supplied join exactly once. Picture join types are cut, dip_to_black, dissolve or other; sound relationships are hard, under, prelap or carries_over. Dialogue entries must reference available takes with valid trim intervals and placement times. Production sound must reference an existing source; explicit timing requires a supplied handle and all timing fields. Required title cards must be declared with nonempty text. A declared music offset must lie inside the supplied cue. The preview must be probeable, contain a video stream, and meet the same total-duration tolerance relative to the locked picture sequence. These structural checks do not by themselves prove that dialogue is intelligible, a declared transition appears in the render, or the mix satisfies the brief; the outcome rubrics judge the actual delivered audiovisual result.

B.5 Isolation and Telemetry

Every trajectory executes in a disposable sandbox without network access. Concurrent rollouts of the same task receive private workspaces, so one sample cannot inspect or overwrite another sample’s output. The environment logs turns, tool calls, images viewed, validation errors, rendering status, and reward components. These records support the later analysis of training cost, failure modes, and credit assignment without enlarging the policy-visible state.

The same public task, observation tools and deliverable contract are used for student training rollouts and evaluation. Reward computations and OPSD teacher-only inputs are performed outside the policy sandbox. They do not enlarge the student’s public state or expose validation answers to it.

Appendix C Training and Evaluation Details

C.1 Training Configuration and Optimization

Training configuration.

Training uses asynchronous policy updates in SkyRL, with FSDP sharding and vLLM inference engines. Table 8 lists the settings shared by every training variant, and Table 9 lists the settings that differ. The periodic validation pass uses one rollout per task to monitor progress. Final reported scores use repeated evaluation of the selected final checkpoint; where available, its recorded validation pass supplies the first repetition and three additional passes complete avg@4. These repetitions vary rollout sampling, not the training seed.

Policy optimization and advantage normalization.

The reward-based variants use token-level importance ratios between the current policy and the rollout policy. Ratios outside (0.8, 1.28)(0.8,\,1.28) receive zero weight; the retained ratios are treated as constants during backpropagation. The policy loss uses token-mean reduction over valid assistant tokens. For Equation 3.3, only valid process scores from turns with active loss tokens enter the group statistics, with ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}. The process advantage is zero for turns with missing or invalid scores, groups with fewer than two valid scores, or groups with sample standard deviation at most ϵ\epsilon; the outcome term is retained.

Process-weight schedule.

The fixed variant uses λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 at every update. For the decayed variant, the coefficient is 0.50.5 through update 20, then 0.5​[1−(u−20)/10]30.5[1-(u-20)/10]^{3} for 20<u<3020<u<30, and zero from update 30 onward. Here uu is the consumer optimizer’s global update index, rather than the index at which an asynchronous rollout began. For example, updates 21 and 25 use coefficients 0.3645 and 0.0625. Setting the coefficient to zero removes the process term from the policy advantage; it does not change the outcome reward or the final evaluation grader.

Token weighting and comparison scope.

The token-mean loss divides the summed contributions of valid assistant tokens by the total number of such tokens in the optimization batch. Thus each valid token has the same reduction weight; turns and trajectories are not individually renormalized to have equal weight. Prompt tokens, tool observations, padding, and positions with an inactive loss mask do not contribute to this loss. The configured batch targets eight trajectories for each of 16 tasks in the reward-based variants and one trajectory for each of 16 tasks in each OPSD variant. Matching 50 updates therefore does not match the number of sampled trajectories or generated tokens across these objectives. The comparisons in this paper are comparisons of the specified training recipes.

C.2 Process-Reward Judgments

Context and timing.

The process judge reviews consecutive windows of ten completed assistant turns; the final window may be shorter. It receives the original public task, public assistant actions and tool observations, registered images, and typed facts derived from the available records. Separate reasoning/thinking fields are excluded from this packet. Target turns and a bounded selection of earlier turns retain detailed evidence; omitted earlier material is explicitly marked as incomplete history. The image packet prioritizes the current window and uses up to 16 original images, reserving at most four for earlier context. These are judge-input limits, not limits on the policy’s observations.

Each window receives three independent judgments from Gemini 3.8 Flash. For a particular turn, valid scores are averaged; an abstention is excluded from this average rather than treated as a neutral vote. If no valid score remains, that turn receives no process contribution. The judge is asked to cite only evidence available at or before the turn being assessed. Since several target turns appear together in a retrospective window, this citation rule does not establish that the model’s judgment is causally independent of later turns in that window.

Evidence validation.

Decisions identify the turn, event type, evidence scope, score, and supporting record IDs. Validators check the allowed fields, event-to-score mapping, record identities and time boundaries. Visual claims require attached pixels; text metadata is not treated as direct auditory evidence. In the archived process-judge adapter, authenticated audio attachments are unavailable, so claims requiring direct listening must abstain unless the available evidence supports a narrower metadata or reasoning judgment. Routine readback of an unchanged JSON file is neutral. The repetition rule is deliberately narrow: it requires the same literal shell command and matching observed text over three consecutive turns, together with evidence that the work is redundant. Such validation checks provenance and protocol compliance; it does not prove semantic correctness or eliminate reward hacking.

C.3 Evaluation and Aggregation

Evaluation configuration.

Table 11 lists the evaluation settings. The outcome grader and the process-reward judge are different models, so process rewards are not produced by the model that assigns the reported outcome scores.

Score aggregation.

For each method and task, avg@4 averages the four outcome scores, rather than selecting the best attempt. Task-type scores then average equally over tasks of that type. Overall averages equally over all 81 tasks: Content Selection has 14 tasks, Narrative Sequencing 15, Rough Cut 26, and Fine Cut 26. Overall is therefore a task-count-weighted average of the four type scores, not their unweighted mean. Relative gains over the base model use the unrounded aggregated scores as (R−Rbase)/Rbase(R-R_{\mathrm{base}})/R_{\mathrm{base}}; the three-decimal scores displayed in the table may not reproduce these percentages exactly. Absolute score differences are likewise computed before rounding.

Interaction length.

Table 12 reports the mean number of turns by task type. A turn is one policy request, counted from the rollout’s recorded request IDs. Each method includes all 324 rollouts from four independent repetitions of the 81 validation tasks, including rollouts whose outcome grades required recovery.

C.4 Behavioral Measurements

The behavioral analysis uses the four recorded validation repetitions of each Qwen3.5-9B variant. Each variant contributes 324 task–repetition pairs. We count a turn from its policy-request identifier, so a request that is interrupted before a completed generation still contributes to interaction length. Tool calls count requested invocations, whereas frames count image attachments returned in completed tool results; these need not increase together. A contact sheet is one image attachment even when it contains multiple sampled frames. Neither measure counts distinct source-film frames. Blind rollouts are those with no returned image attachment. Truncation indicates a recorded budget termination, rather than an assessment of whether the final artifact is correct.

Reasoning length.

Reasoning length is measured in characters, not tokenizer tokens. For each completed generation event, we parse the action text as JSON and read its reasoning field. A missing or non-string field contributes zero characters. We divide the total number of reasoning characters by the number of completed generation events, pooling all tasks and repetitions within a method. This is a turn-weighted average, not the average of per-rollout ratios. It is distinct from the number of policy requests used for interaction length, because an interrupted request may not emit a completed generation event.

Reflection markers.

We apply the case-insensitive expression below to the same reasoning field. A completed turn counts once if any alternative matches, even if several markers occur. The reflection rate is the number of matching turns divided by the number of completed generation events, again pooling tasks and repetitions. Missing reasoning is a non-match. The expression uses Python regular-expression syntax; \b is a word boundary and \s is whitespace.

re.compile(
    r"\bwait[,.\s]"
    r"|\breconsider\b"
    r"|\blet me (re-?check|re-?examine|re-?visit|re-?think|"
    r"re-?do|re-?count|re-?calculate|re-?verify|"
    r"retry|try again)\b"
    r"|\b(was|were|is|are)\s+(wrong|incorrect|invalid)\b"
    r"|\bmy (mistake|error)\b"
    r"|\bshould have\b"
    r"|\b(did|does)\s?n[o’]?t work\b"
    r"|\btry again\b"
    r"|\bon second thought\b"
    r"|\bthat’?s not (right|correct)\b"
    r"|\b(previous|earlier|last) (attempt|approach|try|call)s?\b"
    r"|\bI (over|mis)[a-z]+", re.I)

This is a lexical indicator of explicit reconsideration. It does not establish that the agent found an error, changed its next action, or improved the edit. For example, an isolated “wait” or a mention of a previous attempt can match without an effective correction. Longer reasoning also provides more opportunities for a match. Consequently, the behavior columns describe observed policy activity and should be interpreted together with task outcome and completion, rather than as independent measures of reasoning quality.

C.5 OPSD Teacher Inputs and Diagnostics

Teacher and student.

The KL teacher is a frozen copy of the initial Qwen3.5-9B, initialized from the same checkpoint as the student. It is not updated by an exponential moving average or replaced by the trained student. The student samples its own actions from the public task context. Teacher-side privileged information changes the distribution evaluated at those same student action tokens; it is not inserted into student rollout or evaluation inputs, and it does not replace student actions with supervised action labels.

Reference-answer conditioning.

The private answer card contains the selected clip IDs for Content Selection; the reference order for Narrative Sequencing; and clip-relative reference in/out intervals and target duration for Rough Cut. For Fine Cut it contains reference join decisions, dialogue identities and onset times, and a music source offset. The Fine Cut card is explicitly a partial editing plan, not a ready-to-submit executable edit: unprovided trim endpoints, gains, mixing envelopes and render commands are not invented as reference targets. Rough Cut and Fine Cut reference choices are marked non-unique. The card is inserted only into the teacher’s existing system message while preserving the student’s action-token and image suffix. Cards are bound to training task identities and the corresponding stored answer and manifest; validation tasks are excluded from this private catalog.

Turn-suggestion conditioning.

Gemini 3.8 Flash receives the original public context immediately before turn tt, including prior tool observations and admitted images, and proposes one next action. It neither executes that action nor observes the student’s current action or future outcome. An action may contain multiple tool calls. The proposal is appended as a teacher-only note after the original turn context, followed by the original student action tokens. A separate teacher prefix is constructed for each turn; the note from a previous or future turn is not carried into it. Gemini is the suggestion generator, while the frozen Qwen3.5-9B remains the model that supplies KL targets. Suggestions are checked for format, available tool names, argument schemas and a maximum of 2,048 teacher-hint tokens. These checks do not establish that a suggestion is semantically correct or executable in the student’s state.

Teacher context and objective.

Both variants reserve up to 2,048 additional teacher-only tokens, giving a teacher context limit of 133,120 tokens while the student’s limit remains 131,072. The implemented forward-KL objective uses neither an outcome-reward term nor a process-reward term, and does not apply sampled-action importance weighting. Outcomes are still recorded for evaluation and diagnostics.

Top-KK+tail KL in OPSD.

We give the implemented form of Equation 3.4 here. Let pt,kp_{t,k} and qt,kq_{t,k} be its full-vocabulary student and teacher distributions at token position kk of turn tt. We use uppercase K=64K=64 for the support size, to distinguish it from the token index kk. At each position, the teacher selects

St,k=TopKv∈𝒱⁡qt,k​(v),|St,k|=K.S_{t,k}=\operatorname{TopK}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}q_{t,k}(v),\qquad|S_{t,k}|=K. (C.1)

Both models are evaluated on this same teacher-selected set; the student does not select a separate top-KK set. The selection is made independently at each prediction position on the student’s sampled prefix.

All retained probabilities keep their respective full-vocabulary softmax normalizers. We aggregate the remaining vocabulary into one tail class ⊥\bot, with

qt,k⊥=∑v∉St,kqt,k​(v),pt,k⊥=∑v∉St,kpt,k​(v).q_{t,k}^{\bot}=\sum_{v\notin S_{t,k}}q_{t,k}(v),\qquad p_{t,k}^{\bot}=\sum_{v\notin S_{t,k}}p_{t,k}(v). (C.2)

Thus q~t,k=((qt,k​(v))v∈St,k,qt,k⊥)\widetilde{q}_{t,k}=((q_{t,k}(v))_{v\in S_{t,k}},q_{t,k}^{\bot}) and p~t,k=((pt,k​(v))v∈St,k,pt,k⊥)\widetilde{p}_{t,k}=((p_{t,k}(v))_{v\in S_{t,k}},p_{t,k}^{\bot}) are normalized distributions over the same K+1=65K+1=65 classes. We do not renormalize the retained 64 entries to sum to one or discard the tail mass. The per-token forward KL used in both OPSD variants is

ℓt,k(K)\displaystyle\ell_{t,k}^{(K)} =DKL(q~t,k∥p~t,k)\displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widetilde{q}_{t,k}\|\widetilde{p}_{t,k}) (C.3)
=∑v∈St,kqt,k​(v)​log⁡qt,k​(v)pt,k​(v)+qt,k⊥​log⁡qt,k⊥pt,k⊥.\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in S_{t,k}}q_{t,k}(v)\log\frac{q_{t,k}(v)}{p_{t,k}(v)}+q_{t,k}^{\bot}\log\frac{q_{t,k}^{\bot}}{p_{t,k}^{\bot}}.

The direction is teacher-to-student, DKL(q∥p)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p). The student-sampled token need not belong to St,kS_{t,k}: this is a distribution-level target at every valid assistant prediction position, not a loss evaluated only at the sampled token.

For an optimization batch ℬ\mathcal{B}, let mi,t,k∈{0,1}m_{i,t,k}\in\{0,1\} denote the valid assistant-token loss mask for trajectory ii. The implemented token-mean reduction is

ℒK​(θ)=∑i∈ℬ∑t,kmi,t,k​ℓi,t,k(K)∑i∈ℬ∑t,kmi,t,k.\mathcal{L}_{K}(\theta)=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{t,k}m_{i,t,k}\,\ell_{i,t,k}^{(K)}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{t,k}m_{i,t,k}}. (C.4)

Prompt tokens, tool observations and padding are excluded. Turns and trajectories are not separately normalized to have equal weight. Teacher targets, selected vocabulary IDs and sampled prefixes are held fixed within an update; gradients pass through the student probabilities, including their full-vocabulary normalizer and aggregate tail mass.

Approximation and numerical implementation.

The top-KK+tail construction preserves each selected probability and the total probability outside the selected set. It does not preserve how probability is distributed among individual tail tokens. Its KL is therefore a coarsened objective, rather than the exact full-vocabulary KL; it is no greater than the full KL and becomes equal when the conditional teacher and student distributions within the tail agree.

This construction reduces each stored teacher target to 64 vocabulary IDs and 65 log-probabilities per active position. It does not avoid the full-vocabulary projection needed for normalization. For numerical stability, the implementation computes each tail log-probability as the log-sum-exp of the complementary logits minus the full-vocabulary log-sum-exp, rather than subtracting a near-one retained probability from one. Logits are projected in chunks of 128 active positions, and the backward pass recomputes these projections instead of retaining a trajectory-by-vocabulary tensor. Log-probability arithmetic uses FP32 in the reported runs. We use the same K=64K=64 in both variants and do not claim that this value is optimal or that tail aggregation preserves all full-vocabulary supervision.

Interpreting teacher–student disagreement.

Changing privileged information changes the teacher targets on student-visited states. A larger KL identifies stronger distributional disagreement, but does not by itself establish that the teacher proposes a better action. Likewise, a larger parameter-gradient norm is an observed optimization difference, not proof that a particular probability ratio causes instability. The top-KK+tail forward-KL implementation differentiates through normalized student logits; for a retained vocabulary entry, its logit derivative is the difference between student and teacher probabilities. We therefore interpret the loss, gradient and outcome measurements together, without treating the derivative with respect to an unconstrained probability as a parameter-gradient mechanism.

Gradient magnitude by privileged information.

Table 13 reports the two OPSD mean gradient norms used in Section 6.3, alongside additional diagnostics from the 50 retained optimizer updates. Gradient norms are measured before global clipping. The two OPSD variants and outcome-only GRPO share the learning rate and the clipping threshold. Their objectives, targets, sampled trajectories and evolving policies can all affect the observed norms; this comparison does not isolate a single cause.

How the divergence is spread over a trajectory.

Table 14 uses the 800 trajectories stored in the pre-update signal records (16 per update for 50 updates) of each reported OPSD run. Turns are ranked by their summed token KL, and the table reports the share of total KL held by the top 1% and 5% of turns, and the token share held by the top 5% (rounded down to an integer number of turns). For the last column, turn jj in a trajectory of length LL has relative position j/max⁡(1,L−1)j/\max(1,L-1) with zero-based jj. We average each turn’s per-token KL within the earliest (<0.2<0.2) and latest (≥0.8\geq 0.8) fifths and take their ratio. This diagnostic weights turns equally within each positional bin; it does not change the token-mean training objective.

With reference answers, a median recorded trajectory contains 2323 turns and 13,68013{,}680 generated tokens. Under token-mean reduction, concentrating disagreement in relatively few turns may dilute their contribution when averaged with the remaining tokens. These statistics do not establish whether the divergent turns provide useful guidance or whether this concentration causes the limited performance gains.

Does the target track task success.

For every rollout of every update we take its mean KL per token against the teacher and the outcome reward it earns, which gives 800800 paired values per run over the 50 updates. Table 15 reports the Pearson correlation between the two. This is a descriptive association between distributional disagreement and realized outcome. The observed correlation is modestly negative for reference answers and near zero for turn-level suggestions. Correlation alone neither establishes teacher correctness nor tests whether an individual teacher-guided update improves the student.

C.6 Outcome Metrics and Rubrics

Outcome scoring.

The channel weights (wdet,wref,wblind)(w_{\mathrm{det}},w_{\mathrm{ref}},w_{\mathrm{blind}}) of Equation 4.1 are (1,0,0)(1,0,0) for Content Selection and Narrative Sequencing, (0.4,0.4,0.2)(0.4,0.4,0.2) for Rough Cut, and (0,0.4,0.6)(0,0.4,0.6) for Fine Cut.

Deterministic metrics.

Content Selection uses set F1, 2​|S∩S⋆|/(|S|+|S⋆|)2|S\cap S^{\star}|/(|S|+|S^{\star}|), on the submitted and reference clip IDs. Narrative Sequencing maps the submitted permutation to reference ranks and multiplies three terms: one minus normalized absolute displacement, the length of the longest increasing subsequence divided by the number of clips, and the fraction of consecutive submitted pairs that are consecutive in the reference (Cao et al., 2026). Absolute displacement is normalized by ⌊n2/2⌋\lfloor n^{2}/2\rfloor for nn clips. The Heretic c5 verifier used in our experiments takes the best score over its four accepted orders. Kendall’s τ\tau is logged as a diagnostic but is not the outcome score.

For Rough Cut, a scorable shot is a hit only if both its in-point error and its retained-duration error fall within the corresponding reference tolerances. The deterministic score is the fraction of scorable shots that are hits. In-point tolerances are shot-specific, derived from the alignment’s self-similarity plateau; retained-duration tolerance comes from the task key. Unmatched alternate takes remain in the delivered sequence but are excluded from this reference-based denominator. Invalid ranges are not exempted as unscorable shots. Fine Cut has no deterministic similarity channel.

The two judge channels are rubric-based, and Table 16 lists their items. A separate multimodal judgment grades each subjective item from 0 to 4 using the submitted continuous video and the relevant evidence. Rough Cut additionally has a mechanically assigned duration band in its reference channel. The item scores combine into a channel score by

Rchannel=∑isi​wi4​∑iwi​(0.75)z,R_{\mathrm{channel}}=\frac{\sum_{i}s_{i}w_{i}}{4\sum_{i}w_{i}}\,(0.75)^{z}, (C.5)

where zz counts the items that scored 0. The factor (0.75)z(0.75)^{z} is a soft penalty. The final evaluation uses direct rubric judgments with submission validation enabled; no additional joint consistency-review call modifies the channel scores. A complete Rough Cut grade comprises six subjective rubric judgments plus mechanical metrics; a Fine Cut grade comprises seven subjective rubric judgments. These counts describe distinct items, not provider requests after transport or output-format retries. Missing required grades are recorded as grading failures rather than silently renormalizing the remaining channels.

What each rubric evaluates.

Tables 17 and 18 specify the individual criteria. The task prompt establishes the required visual beat and audiovisual functions. The public manifest identifies the available assets and their time coordinates. Reference-informed judgments additionally receive reference evidence, but a reference choice does not by itself make that choice mandatory. A different edit can receive full credit when it satisfies the task. Judges must ground their assessment in the submitted continuous video and audio, using clip or join IDs and timestamps to locate the evidence. Contact sheets, source context, ASR, and signal measurements support inspection; they do not replace watching and listening to the submission. A missing measurement means unknown, and an empty defect list is not sufficient evidence of quality.

For the mechanical RC duration item, each percentage threshold is replaced by the larger of that percentage of the target and the answer key’s dur_tol_s; the implementation uses 0.1668 seconds if that field is absent or zero. The band is computed arithmetically without an LLM call. This item measures total duration, whereas the separate deterministic RC score tests both in-point and kept-duration tolerances shot by shot. These two uses of timing should not be conflated with the validity checks applied before judging.

The subjective rubrics distinguish full satisfaction from minor, repeated, major, and fundamental failures using the criterion-specific conditions in these tables. They do not introduce a common numeric threshold for dialogue loudness, bridge counts, shot-length variation, or source-reference distance. The highest band requires positive evidence that the stated criterion is met; a lower band requires an observable, task-relevant defect. Reference media is used only when actually available to the judge, and source annotations or declared edit notes cannot establish that their contents occur in the submitted render.

Rubric interpretation.

The blind Rough Cut rubric assesses useful picture entry/exit points, coverage of the requested visual beat, and continuity of the actual joins. Its reference channel assesses entries, exits and pacing with the released edit as a feasible comparison. Fine Cut evaluates delivered dialogue, music, audiovisual continuity choices and transition execution; its reference channel revisits dialogue, continuity and music. In all subjective rubrics, band 4 denotes full task-appropriate compliance, band 3 a minor defect, band 2 several or a meaningful defect, band 1 substantial failure, and band 0 failure of an essential requirement. The per-item criteria specify the relevant visible or audible defect; this summary is not an additional scoring rule. Appropriate silence, a hard cut, or an alternative edit is not penalized merely for differing from the reference. Declarations, tool counts, source transcripts and metadata alone do not prove a successful delivered result.

Rough Cut duration band.

Let TT be the target duration and EE the absolute error in the summed retained clip durations. The mechanical reference-channel item assigns bands 4, 3, 2, and 1 when EE is at most 3%, 8%, 18%, and 35% of TT, respectively; each threshold has an absolute floor equal to the task’s frame-based duration tolerance. Larger errors receive band 0. This graded item is separate from the common submission-validity gate, which allows total-duration error max⁡(1,min⁡(3,0.1​T))\max(1,\min(3,0.1T)) seconds. A submission outside that gate receives zero outcome reward before subjective quality can contribute.

Scoring exclusions.

The protocol accepts the first valid grade rather than the best available one. In the initial evaluation pass, judge refusals are not retried. Both rules avoid selecting for trajectories that happen to score well on a later attempt. Refusals are rare but not absent: a small number of Rough Cut trajectories trigger the judge’s content filter, which excludes that trajectory and the group it belongs to. Where this leaves a repetition incomplete we average over the remaining complete repetitions and report the count. For the six Qwen3.5-9B variants reported in Table 3, recovered grades fill the initially excluded evaluations, giving complete coverage of all 324 task–repetition pairs per variant. Behavioral metrics for Qwen3.5-9B cover all four repetitions of the 81 validation tasks (Table 5).

C.7 Additional Training Diagnostics

The following curves use optimizer-update metric records. Their logged generation counts can differ from the fixed-size OPSD signal exports analyzed above; interaction length uses the logged batch denominator. Averages over update ranges give each recorded update equal weight.

Process-reward dynamics.

Figure 3 expands the process- and outcome-reward curves shown in Figure 1(c).

Training dynamics beyond the final evaluation.

Figure 4 reports the outcome reward and interaction length of the training batches for the five Qwen3.5-9B variants. These are training diagnostics, separate from the repeated held-out evaluation. Over updates 41–50, GRPO+PRM (fixed λ\lambda) averages 80.5 policy turns per rollout, compared with 43.8 for outcome-only GRPO and 60.7 for GRPO+PRM (decayed λ\lambda); the corresponding means of the per-update outcome rewards are 0.257, 0.356, and 0.394. Thus, the longer trajectories of the fixed-weight run do not coincide with higher training outcome reward in this interval. These lengths do not measure truncation or successful task completion.

Observed degradation in OPSD (turn-level suggestions).

The outcome and generation diagnostics make the degradation visible beyond the training objective. In OPSD (turn-level suggestions), mean training outcome reward decreases from 0.166 over updates 1–10 to 0.020 over updates 41–50, while mean generated assistant tokens per rollout decrease from 13.9k to 2.9k. For OPSD (reference answers), the corresponding outcome means are 0.255 and 0.245. Figure 5 shows larger teacher–student KL and gradient norms, together with generally lower later policy entropy, for the suggestion-conditioned run. Its gradient norm exceeds 1.0 on 22 of the 50 retained updates, compared with none for the reference-conditioned run. These observations document degradation in this configuration; they do not isolate its cause. The comparisons involve different sampled trajectories, and the OPSD variants use one rollout per task while the reward-based variants use eight.
